1.q: הוֹד֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה כִּי־ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְ⁠עוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽ⁠וֹ
1.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 106:1.

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [thank Yahweh for his covenant faithfulness is to forever]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he remains faithful to his covenant]

The psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “without end.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [lasts throughout eternity]

2.note: Here, **Israel** represents the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Let the people of Israel indeed say]

The psalmist is saying what he wants **Israel** to do. See the discussion in the introduction to Psalms about “let” and “may” and follow the decision of your team of how a speaker will express in this context what he wants someone to do. Alternate translation: [May Israel indeed say]
See how you translated this in the previous verse.

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [We praise Yahweh for his covenant faithfulness is to forever]

3.note: Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Aaron** figuratively means all the people descended from Aaron, who was the first high priest. Alternate translation: [Let the descendants of Aaron indeed say]
See how you translated this in the previous verse.

4.note: See how you translated this in the previous verse.

5.note: The psalmist is using **From the constriction** as a common expression of the culture to mean “from a distressing situation” or “from a time of trouble.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [From between a rock and a hard place] or [From a distressing situation]
The word **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh.” Alternate translation: [I called out to Yahweh and he answered me]

The psalmist is using **with wideness** as a common expression of the culture to mean “by setting me free” or “by relieving my distressing situation.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yah set me in a wide place] or [Yah answered me by relieving my distressing situation]

6.note: The psalmist is using **Yahweh is for me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh supports me” or “Yahweh is on my side.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh wants me to succeed]

The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [man do nothing to harm me]

7.note: The psalmist is using **Yahweh is for me as my helper** as a common expression of the culture to mean “Yahweh wants me to succeed and so he helps me.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh wants me to succeed and so he helps me]

The psalmist is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I will gaze** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize his personal commitment to triumph over his enemies. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and so for my part, I will gaze]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **haters**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [on those who hate me]

8.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were a **shelter** that people could go into for protection from danger. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to let Yahweh protect us]

The psalmist is not referring to a specific **man**. He means people in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [than to trust in people]

9.note: See how you translated this phrase in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [to let Yahweh protect us]

10.note: The psalmist says **All the nations** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [It seemed as though all the nations] or [So many nations]

Here, **name** represents the power and authority of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by Yahweh’s power]

The word translated as **I fended them off** could mean: (1) the psalmist’s army pushed back the other armies. Alternate translation: [I defeated them] or it could be a different word that is spelled the same way that means: (2) the psalmist’s army circumcised the enemy armies. Alternate translation: [I circumcised them] or [I cut them off]

11.note: The expressions **They surrounded me** and **yes, they surrounded me** mean the same thing. The psalmist is using repetition for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [They had me completely surrounded]
See how you translated this in the previous verse.

12.note: The psalmist is making a comparison between his enemies and **bees**. The point of this comparison is that just as **bees** swarm around aggressively when attacking, so his enemies surrounded him aggressively. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They surrounded me like bees do when they are attacking someone]

The expression **they were extinguished** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they died away quickly like a fire burning thorns]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a fire of thorns** burns out quickly, so the psalmist’s enemies **were extinguished** quickly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [they were extinguished as quickly as is a fire among thorns]
See how you translated this in verse 10.

13.note: The psalmist is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this. Alternate translation: [You pushed me down hard]

Here, **to fall** marks this clause as the goal or purpose of **To push down, you pushed me down**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [so that I would fall]

Here the psalmist is speaking of his enemies’ attack as if the enemies were able to **push** him **down** physically to make him **fall**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison. Alternate translation: [You attacked me violently in order to defeat me]

The psalmist is speaking to his enemies that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about how violently they attacked him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about **his enemies**. Alternate translation: [My enemies attacked me violently in order to defeat me]

14.note: **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers as modeled in the UST.
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **strength** and **song**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [Yah makes me strong and joyful]

Here, **song** represents “a reason to sing” or “joy.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Yah gives me strength and the joy to sing]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and he saves me]

15.note: The phrase **a shout and salvation** expresses a single idea. The word **shout** tells more about **salvation**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [The voice of a victorious shout]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]
The psalmist may be quoting a song of victory, starting here and going through verse 16. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark this as the beginning of a song, as in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **valor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the right hand of Yahweh does valiant things]

Here, **right hand** represents the power of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the power of Yahweh]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **valor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [valiant things]

16.note: The psalmist is using **The right hand of Yahweh is high** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Yahweh is superior to all others or that Yahweh is victorious. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is superior to all others]
See how you translated this phrase in the previous verse.

17.note: The psalmist uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between dying and living. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I will not die; instead, I will live]
The word **Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh.” Alternate translation: [of Yahweh]

18.note: The psalmist is repeating forms of the verb **chastise** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [Yah has certainly chastised me]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers as modeled in the UST.

Here the psalmist is speaking of **death** as if it were a place or person that Yahweh could give him **to**. He means that Yahweh has not allowed him to die. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but he has kept me alive]

19.note: The word translated as **Open** is a plural command form, addressed to the keepers of the gates, which could refer to (1) the gates of the temple, or (2) the gates of Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could include the addressees, as in the UST.

Here, **righteousness** could refer to (1) the people who are allowed to enter through the gates (as indicated in the next verse), which could be either the gates of the temple or the gates of Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [the gates where the righteous may enter] or (2) Yahweh, who is righteous and who dwells in the temple. Alternate translation: [the gates of the temple of the righteous God]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers as modeled in the UST.

20.note: The psalmist may be quoting the response of the gatekeeper in this verse. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark this as a quotation, as in the UST.

Here, **the gate of Yahweh** probably does refer to the gate of the temple, and could mean (1) the gate belonging to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [the gate that belongs to Yahweh] or (2) the gate that leads to Yahweh. Alternate translation: [the gate to where Yahweh dwells]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

21.note: The psalmist switches to addressing Yahweh directly using **you** in this verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could continue using the third person here. Alternate translation: [I will thank Yahweh, for he answered me, and he has become salvation for me]

The psalmist is using **answered me** as a common expression of the culture to mean “acted on my behalf” in response to a request. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for you acted on my behalf]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and you have saved me]

22.q: אֶ֭בֶן מָאֲס֣וּ הַ⁠בּוֹנִ֑ים הָ֝יְתָ֗ה לְ⁠רֹ֣אשׁ פִּנָּֽה
22.note: This is likely a proverb that the psalmist has used to describe either himself or the nation of Israel. If possible, translate this proverb in a way that will be recognized as a proverb and be meaningful in your language and culture. Otherwise, you could give the plain meaning. Alternate translation: [That which others have considered worthless, Yahweh has made to be the most important]

By **the head of the corner**, the psalmist means the cornerstone, which is the most important stone that holds a building together. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the cornerstone]

23.q: מֵ⁠אֵ֣ת יְ֭הוָה הָ֣יְתָה זֹּ֑את הִ֖יא נִפְלָ֣את בְּ⁠עֵינֵֽי⁠נוּ
23.note: The psalmist may be quoting the response of the congregation to the psalmist in verses 23–27. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark this as a quotation, as in the UST.

The pronoun **This** refers to the rejected stone becoming the most important stone, as described in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [This reversal from rejection to victory is from Yahweh]

The psalmist is using **it is marvelous in our eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “we consider it to be a marvelous thing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we consider it to be a marvelous thing]

24.note: The psalmist is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time when God acted to bring about the events being celebrated. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh caused the events we are celebrating today to happen]

The terms **rejoice** and **be glad** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [Let us rejoice greatly]

25.note: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [save us please]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [give us success please]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **success**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [enable us to succeed please]

26.note: The expression **Blessed is** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [Yahweh blesses the one coming]

Here, **name** represents the power and authority of Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with the authority of Yahweh]

The word **you** is plural here because the psalmist is addressing all the people who have come to the temple. So use the plural form in your translation if your language marks that distinction. Alternate translation: [we bless you all]

The psalmist is speaking of the temple of Yahweh as if it were a **house** in which he lived. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from the temple of Yahweh]

27.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of God’s favor and blessing as if it were **light** that God had given to them. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he has given us success]
Here the psalmist ends his quotation of the people. You may want to indicate this with closing quote marks, as in the UST.

28.note: Here the psalmist is speaking of praising God as if it were **exalting** him or lifting him up to a high position. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will publicly praise you]

29.q: הוֹד֣וּ לַ⁠יהוָ֣ה כִּי־ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְ⁠עוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽ⁠וֹ
29.note: See how you translated this in Psalm 106:1 and 118:1.

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [give thanks to Yahweh for his covenant faithfulness is to forever]

The psalmist is using **to forever** as a common expression of his culture to mean “eternally” or “without end.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for his covenant faithfulness lasts forever]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he remains faithful to his covenant forever]
